identity.topic: What If 10 Business Titans Went Broke? Five Years to Prove It Wasn't Luck: ten real living business people lose everything on one courthouse bench and must earn without credit for five years
identity.format: production_script/3 dialogue mini-film, about 13 minutes, 2D hand-drawn caricatures; the narrator and the invented Vance are voiced, the real people speak in speech bubbles (D-62); 10 Shorts
identity.audience: US general audience, adults and teens, English; viewers who follow business personalities and argue about whether the rich earned it
identity.audience_value: the viewer finally sees the skill-versus-luck argument played out instead of asserted, with each titan's public persona tested by one concrete problem
identity.central_question: Strip ten famous fortunes down to what is inside their heads and take away every lender: was their money ever skill, or was it luck?
identity.unique_angle: credit is the hidden variable: people who can build or sell with their own hands recover, people whose deals ran on other people's trust stall, and the real winner is the one who bought a small piece of everyone for forty dollars
identity.tone: dry, fast situational comedy with real stakes; a documentary of events happening now (D-61)
identity.emotional_arc: schadenfreude on the bench, curiosity at the first hustles, dread as the promise of 500 outruns the parts, shock at the fire, respect at Belfort's refusal, satisfaction at the honest win, and a twist that reframes everything
identity.stakes: riders' safety and the heroes' last dollar against a buyer offering riches for silence
identity.payoff: luck decided which envelope paid; skill decided who was still standing when it did, and the man who never built anything owns a piece of eight of them
identity.beyond_a_summary: it is not a list of billionaire origin stories: it is an invented controlled experiment (same start, no credit) that isolates one mechanism, trust as capital, and lets the viewer watch it decide outcomes

viewer_takeaway.understand: a loan is a stranger's trust with interest on top; without it, only what you can make or sell today counts, and a diversified small stake can beat a heroic single bet
viewer_takeaway.feel: the pull of the cover-up offer and the relief when the one man with a fraud conviction refuses it
viewer_takeaway.question: which of the ten would I have been, and would I have signed O'Leary's envelope?
viewer_takeaway.remember: forty dollars, ten percent, forever, and the man who read the envelope to the last line

risks.element: The invented buyer 'Vance', who proposes hiding the fire's cause (S12, SH07)
risks.evidence: Vance is invented (cast.vance: grey suit, grey tie, grey smile; voice 'Silas - Weathered Villain'), but the surname is that of the sitting US Vice President, JD Vance, and the same video stars the sitting president; S12 and Short SH07 put the name on screen ('holds out a card. Vance.'). Re-checked 2026-10-20 after D-62: Vance is now one of only two voiced characters; his voice 'Silas' is a library voice whose style names no person and describes no real official's voice, and his card (grey suit, grey tie, grey smile) does not resemble one, so the creator's decision still holds as recorded.
risks.rationale: US viewers in 2026 are likely to hear the name as a wink at the Vice President, which would turn the story's only fraudster into an implied real official proposing a cover-up: that pulls the episode into politics (ER-08, advertiser suitability), invites a reading of false implication about a real person, and puts an ElevenLabs voice on a character some will read as an elected official (ER-03). The name was chosen creatively and the drawing does not resemble him, so how strongly viewers make the link is uncertain; the creator decides.
risks.mitigation: Decided (creator 2026-10-20): keep 'Vance' as written; his drawing and voice stay far from any real official (ER-08). Options that were offered: Recommended: rename the invented buyer to a surname with no prominent living public figure behind it (one word in S12, SH07 and cast.vance; a re-approval of those lines under OR-17). Alternative: keep 'Vance' with a recorded decision that the link is acceptable, and keep his drawing far from any real official.

decision.answer: Keep the name Vance as written; he is an invented character and nothing in the script ties him to any real person.

Google generative AI policy re-read 2026-10-20 (B-11, V-57): it bars impersonating a person 'in order to deceive' (4.2), circumventing safety filters (2.3) and IP or privacy violations; it has no clause against depicting public figures. With drawn exaggeration in the channel's one style and ER-07's no-photo rule, no material issue found.

risks.element: Speech bubbles carrying the invented lines of seven real people (Trump, Musk, Belfort, O'Leary, Kiyosaki, Cuban, Bezos) in the long video and the Shorts (D-62)

The words are the same invented dialogue already assessed in RK-03..RK-09; the description's notice says every line of dialogue is invented and nobody named took part (ER-06). YouTube 2801947 targets a likeness or voice that falsely implies authorisation or a fake speech passed off as real; Hustler v. Falwell (V-53); Georgia Arts. 1(e), 4 (V-55).
risks.rationale: A drawn speech bubble over a caricature is the oldest form of satirical cartoon and cannot be taken for a recording of the person, so moving the lines from a voice to bubbles removes the provider-terms problem without adding a new one. No material issue found, provided the bubble texts stay the approved lines (ER-02) and contain no political content (ER-08).
